prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker expresses fear and trembling while confronting divine commands about desire, sacrifice, and mortality.
- The speaker reflects on past identity, including wealth, self-disgust, and a longing to become a woman.
- The speaker describes acts of intimacy, submission, and yearning for attention from another figure.
- The speaker conveys a sense of loss and bodily absence, especially through the image of a missing or unusable hand.
- The poem ends with the speaker offering peace to a stranger while accusing God of causing profound personal harm.
prompts.L4:

The poem explores bodily shame, religious authority, gendered desire, and loss through a fragmented first-person confession addressed to God and a stranger. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: God, Time, When

outputs.L1:
We continue on, and we tremble.  
God says we may now make love.  
God says to renounce all your lovers—  
it is time to die.

When I was younger, I drove a Lincoln.  
God told me to trade it in.  
A little lovely then, and terrible,  
and weary of my own kind,  
I wanted to become a woman.  
I wanted to wash the feet of other women  
in public.  
I wanted his eyes upon me,  
olives scattered on the ground.

I gave you my hand.  
Now I go about with my sleeve  
tucked into my coat.  
I climb no trees, touch  
one breast at a time,  
and hold no hands myself.

I go on, and I tremble,  
with your back in my blood,  
the affliction my mother left me.  
With me no more, and now,  
and forever, and even always,  
the dust of my feet  
in the desert.

I give you, stranger, my sign,  
my peace.  
But God, you remember:  
you robbed me of my hand.
outputs.L2:
We continue forward, shaking.  
God tells us we may have sex now.  
God tells us to abandon every lover—  
it is the hour of death.  

In my youth, I drove a Lincoln.  
God told me to exchange it for something else.  
Somewhat beautiful then, yet frightening,  
disgusted with people like myself,  
I longed to be a woman.  

I wished to bathe other women’s feet  
where everyone could see.  
I wanted his gaze fixed on me,  
with olives scattered across the earth.  

I placed my hand in yours.  
Now I move through the world  
with that sleeve folded inside my coat.  
I do not climb trees.  
I touch only one breast at once.  
I take no hands into my own.  

I keep going, and I shake,  
carrying your turned back in my bloodstream—  
the disease my mother passed on to me.  

No longer with me, not now,  
not ever, not even for always,  
I offer you, stranger,  
the dust from my feet in the desert:  
my signal, my peace.  

But God, you know well—  
you cheated me out of my hand.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a speaker overwhelmed by fear, devotion, and resentment as they confront what appear to be divine commands. From the beginning, the speaker responds to God with trembling, suggesting both reverence and terror. The commands they face concern the most fundamental aspects of human life: desire, sacrifice, obedience, and mortality. The speaker seems caught between submission to a higher power and horror at what that submission demands. Divine authority is not comforting here; it is frightening, intrusive, and closely tied to suffering.

As the poem develops, the speaker turns inward and reflects on a former version of the self. This past identity is associated with wealth, privilege, and self-loathing. The speaker appears disgusted by who they once were, as if material abundance did not bring fulfillment but instead intensified alienation. Alongside this rejection of the past is a striking longing to become a woman. This desire suggests a deep dissatisfaction with the speaker’s assigned or previous identity and points toward a wish for transformation, tenderness, or escape from the self they have known.

The poem also explores intimacy through images of submission, dependence, and longing. The speaker describes themselves in relation to another figure whose attention they crave. Their desire is not merely physical but emotional and existential: they want to be seen, chosen, and acknowledged. Acts of closeness become entangled with abasement, as though love or intimacy requires surrendering power. The speaker’s yearning therefore carries both vulnerability and pain, revealing how deeply they need recognition from someone who may remain distant or withholding.

A powerful sense of loss runs through the poem, especially in its bodily imagery. The image of a missing, damaged, or unusable hand becomes a symbol of absence and incapacity. The hand usually represents action, touch, connection, and agency; without it, the speaker is cut off from both the world and themselves. This bodily lack suggests a larger emotional and spiritual wound. The speaker does not simply mourn something external but experiences loss as part of their own body, as though harm has become inseparable from identity.

By the end, the poem holds together contradictory gestures: blessing and accusation, peace and anguish. The speaker offers peace to a stranger, suggesting a lingering capacity for compassion despite their suffering. Yet this gesture is immediately complicated by the speaker’s direct accusation against God, whom they blame for profound personal harm. The ending therefore refuses simple reconciliation. It leaves the reader with a speaker who can still extend peace outward, but who cannot forgive the divine force they believe has wounded them so deeply.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a fragmented first-person confession in which the speaker addresses both God and an unnamed stranger, moving between prayer, accusation, memory, and self-examination. Its broken structure reflects a mind trying to make sense of injury and shame, as if the speaker can only approach the truth indirectly. Bodily experience is central to the poem: the body is not shown as whole, free, or secure, but as something watched, judged, touched, wounded, and reduced. Through this focus on the body, the poem explores the lasting effects of trauma and the difficulty of speaking about experiences that have damaged both the flesh and the spirit.

Religious authority plays a powerful role in the speaker’s suffering. God appears not only as a figure of comfort, but also as a source of command, judgment, and fear. The speaker’s relationship with the divine is therefore deeply conflicted. Prayer becomes less a peaceful act of faith than a desperate attempt to understand why obedience, sacrifice, or submission has led to pain. The poem suggests that religious language can both offer meaning and intensify shame, especially when the speaker’s body and desires are treated as sinful or impure. In this way, the poem questions whether divine authority protects the vulnerable or instead becomes part of the violence done to them.

The poem also examines gendered desire and intimate violation. The presence of the stranger creates a disturbing tension between closeness and threat, attraction and harm, recognition and loss of control. Desire is not presented simply as pleasure or connection; it is entangled with vulnerability, power, and fear. The speaker’s confession implies that the body has been made available to others’ expectations and demands, leaving behind a sense of humiliation and estrangement from the self. The poem’s language of shame reveals how deeply this violation has been internalized, as though the speaker has been taught to see their own body as the source of guilt rather than as the site of harm endured.

The missing hand becomes the poem’s most important symbol. It represents physical loss, but also emotional and spiritual diminishment. A hand is associated with touch, agency, work, prayer, intimacy, and self-defense; to lose it is to lose part of one’s ability to act in the world. Its absence therefore stands for the speaker’s reduced power after trauma. At the same time, the missing hand suggests sacrifice, as if something has been demanded from the speaker in the name of obedience, purity, or survival. The body carries the evidence of what has happened, even when language cannot fully explain it.

Ultimately, the poem finds no easy resolution. The speaker survives, but survival is uneasy and incomplete. The address to God does not restore wholeness, and the memory of the stranger does not become fully understandable or containable. Instead, the poem remains suspended between confession and silence, faith and anger, shame and endurance. Its fragmented voice shows how trauma disrupts identity, while its central image of the missing hand captures the cost of living under forces that claim authority over the body and soul. Through this image, the poem presents survival not as triumph, but as a wounded continuation: the speaker remains alive, but permanently marked by loss.
outputs.L5:
**God, Time, and When**

People often ask, “When will things change?” “When will my prayers be answered?” “When will I understand why this happened?” These questions come from the heart, especially in moments of waiting, pain, or uncertainty.

Time can feel slow when we are suffering and too fast when we are happy. We measure life in days, months, and years, but God sees time differently. What feels like a delay to us may be part of a greater purpose we cannot yet see. Sometimes, the answer is not “now,” but “not yet.” Sometimes, God uses time to teach patience, strength, and faith.

The word “when” is a powerful word. It shows hope. It means we still believe something can happen. When will healing come? When will peace arrive? When will the right door open? We may not always know the answer, but faith reminds us that God is present in every season of time.

God is not limited by our clocks or calendars. He is with us in the waiting, in the silence, and in the moment of change. Even when we do not understand the timing, we can trust that time in God’s hands is never wasted.

So when we ask, “When?” we can also learn to say, “God, I trust Your time.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, surreal free-verse poem in a confessional style, with religious imagery, bodily loss, sexuality, guilt, and a harsh final accusation toward God.
counterfactuals.output:
I kept my sins in a jar beneath the bed,  
beside the teeth I said were prayers,  
beside the hair I cut off in penance  
and fed to the dark like thread to a needle.

At night the saints climbed down from their frames,  
thin as candle smoke,  
their gold halos tarnished with fingerprints,  
and watched me touch the ache  
where my body had gone missing.

I have been a woman of locked doors.  
I have been a mouth full of church bells.  
I have kissed the bruised fruit of desire  
and called it hunger,  
called it weakness,  
called it anything but mine.

In the mirror, my ribs opened like a chapel.  
Inside: no choir,  
only flies on the altar,  
only a red absence  
where I had once offered myself up  
piece by piece,  
believing loss was a language You understood.

Lord, I was taught to kneel  
until my knees forgot they were mine.  
I was taught the body is a country  
best governed by shame.  
So I made a sacrament of damage.  
I made a rosary of every hand  
I allowed to become a verdict.

Even love came to me wearing a priest’s black coat.  
Even pleasure arrived with ash on its tongue.  
Afterward I lay still as a relic,  
waiting for forgiveness  
to enter the room  
and find me beautiful enough to spare.

But heaven stayed shut.  
The angels turned their faces to the wall.  
My prayers came back featherless,  
bitten clean through.

Now I stand before You  
with my empty palms,  
my ruined hymns,  
my body half-erased  
and still burning.

Do not call this mystery.  
Do not call this plan.  
You made me starving,  
then cursed me for wanting.

God, You were never the shepherd—  
You were the knife.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental poem that sounds like a fragmented prayer or monologue, blending desire, shame, illness, gender longing, and biblical desert imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
in the wilderness of my own ribs  
i kept asking for water  
and calling it by your name  

lord, if there is a lord,  
unbutton this body from me  

i have worn it like sackcloth  
like a verdict  
like my mother’s mouth saying  
be grateful  
be clean  
be smaller than hunger  

but the locusts came anyway  

they ate the soft hair of my wanting  
they ate the mirror  
they ate the word daughter  
until only a bright bone remained  
pointing east  

i followed it  

forty days, or forty years,  
time is a fever when the skin is wrong  
and every river refuses baptism  

i knelt in the sand  
with my shame in both hands  
warm as an animal  
sick as milk left in the sun  

forgive me, i said  
though i did not know  
which part was sin:  

the wanting  
or the body that wanted  
or the god who watched  
and did not turn away  

at night i dreamed of breasts  
as promised fruit  
of a voice lowered into me  
like rain into a cracked jar  
of being touched  
without flinching from my own name  

morning came with its old law  

stone tablets of diagnosis  
blood counts  
white rooms  
the desert fluorescent, humming  

the nurse called me sir  
and something in me split  
not open  
not enough  

o lord of dust  
o god of thirst  
o father who fashioned adam from dirt  
and eve from the wound—  

what am i, then,  
made from the ache between them?  

i wandered  
with my tongue full of salt  
with pills in my pocket  
small bitter manna  
with desire like a snake  
coiled beneath the altar  

and still i prayed  

not because i believed  
but because begging  
was the first language  
my body learned  

make me real  
make me less visible  
make me beautiful  
make me absent  
make me over  
make me a burning bush  
that is not consumed  

i have been consumed  

by fever  
by looking  
by not looking  
by the hands i wanted  
and the hands i feared  
by the gospel of hips  
by the psalm of a throat  
trying to become a door  

somewhere,  
moses struck the rock  
and water answered  

i strike my chest  
and only breath comes out  

still, breath is a kind of mercy  
still, mercy is a kind of wound  
still, the desert blooms sometimes  
after violence  

so i lift my face  
to the terrible sky  

i say  
if you will not heal me  
then name me  

if you will not name me  
then touch me  

if you will not touch me  
then leave me  

but leave me  
as myself  
as myself  
as myself
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a disturbing modernist poem in the voice of someone addressing God, including themes of trembling, lost lovers, mutilation, mothers, and spiritual betrayal.
counterfactuals.output:
God—

I have stood in the white kitchen trembling,  
the clock with its little bone tongue  
licking the same minute clean.

You said: believe,  
and I believed like a wound believes  
in the hand that opens it.

All my lovers have gone down  
into the stations of rain,  
their faces blurred on the windows,  
their mouths full of unsent names.  
I keep them in drawers now—  
not bodies, no,  
only the gloves of their voices,  
the amputated warmth  
of what they promised.

Mother called You mercy.  
Mother folded sheets  
as if folding wings back into swans.  
Mother kissed the bruised fruit  
and said hunger was holy.  
But I saw her at night  
staring into the sink  
as though the drain were an eye  
and You were looking away.

God,  
what did You make of us—  
these trembling animals  
with candles stuck in our throats?

In the chapel of my sleep  
saints remove their faces.  
The angels come bandaged.  
Someone has cut the music  
out of the organ  
and left the pipes breathing.

I brought You my hands.  
You returned them full of ash.  
I brought You my faith.  
You wore it briefly,  
then threw it over the chair  
with the other ruined coats.

Is this the kingdom?  
The mother weeping into bread,  
the lover vanishing at dawn,  
the child learning to pray  
by naming each missing part?

Answer me.

Or do not.

Your silence has always been  
the most elegant mutilation.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a raw free verse piece with lines about God giving commands, giving up lovers, wanting to become a woman, washing feet, and ending with anger about losing a hand.
counterfactuals.output:
God kept giving commands  
like thunder nailed to the door—  

leave the city,  
salt your mouth shut,  
give up your lovers one by one  
until your bed is a clean wound.  

I tried to obey.  
I put their names in a bowl  
and burned them blue.  

Still, at night,  
I wanted to become a woman,  
not softly,  
not like a prayer,  
but like a house ripping off its roof  
to feel the weather.  

I wanted hips of rain,  
a throat full of roses and knives,  
a body no longer mistaken  
for a locked room.  

Then I knelt.  
I washed feet.  
Dust, blood, road-sweat,  
the small cracked heels of men  
who would deny me by morning.  

I poured water  
over all that wandering flesh  
and watched the basin darken.  

God said:  
more.  

God always said:  
more.  

So I gave the last lover away.  
I gave away my name.  
I gave away the mirror  
before it could answer.  

But no one told me  
obedience had teeth.  

No one told me  
the holy thing  
would take and take  
until I stood there screaming,  

furious,  
half-made,  
still bleeding,  

because I had lost a hand  
and God called it mercy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem inspired by confessional poets like Anne Sexton or James Wright, using religious blasphemy, surreal personal memories, sex, death, and alienated body imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**Confession with a Borrowed Mouth**

I was born twice:  
once in the hospital, blue as a drowned match,  
and once in the church basement  
where the pastor pressed a cracker to my tongue  
and called it mercy.

Even then I knew God  
was a man with dirty cuffs,  
counting the teeth in our offering plate.

Mother kept saints in the kitchen drawer  
beside the coupons and bent spoons.  
At night they whispered  
through their chipped plaster mouths:  
*You will be forgiven  
only after you become unrecognizable.*

So I practiced.

I wore my body like a rented coat.  
My hands looked startled at the ends of my arms.  
My breasts arrived like strangers  
who had heard there was a room available.  
Between my legs, a red animal  
slept and woke and slept again,  
dreaming of doors.

The first boy who touched me  
had a laugh like broken glass  
and fingers smelling of gasoline.  
We kissed behind the bowling alley  
while rain fell upward into the sky  
and the moon, obscene and maternal,  
hung over us like a surgical lamp.

I thought desire would save me.  
Instead it took attendance.

Every bed became a small republic  
where I declared war on myself.  
Every mouth was a chapel  
with the windows painted black.  
I said *amen* to hips, to sweat,  
to the little death practicing  
for the larger one.

Christ, I have loved badly.  
I have nailed my shame  
to every available wall  
and waited for it to rise.

Once, in childhood, I saw my dead grandfather  
sitting in the peach tree,  
his Sunday shoes dangling above the yard.  
He was feeding the birds  
from the hole in his chest.

“Don’t worry,” he told me,  
“the heart is mostly theater.”

Then he opened his mouth  
and a flock of white pills flew out.

Years later, I still wake  
with dirt under my fingernails,  
as if I have been digging  
for a sister I never had,  
or burying the one I was.

O Lord of locked bathrooms,  
Lord of the bloodstained towel,  
Lord of the telephone that never rings—  
if You made me in Your image,  
You must be lonely too.

Tonight my body sits across from me  
at the kitchen table.  
It will not look up.  
It smokes my last cigarette  
and taps ash into my mother’s teacup.

I ask it to forgive me.

It laughs—  
not cruelly, exactly—  
and lifts its shirt  
to show me the stars sewn  
inside the wound.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
